sources.note: Phonology tables cover the Western (standard Jiwei) dialect only; nothing on stress; gives the Eastern subdialect list (tuyu 4 Xiaozhang, 5 Danqing, 6 Dengshang) after Yang 2004 and Li & Li 2012, and the bibliography (Sposato 2015/2021, Xiang 1999, Yang 2004, 2017).

sources.citation: Sposato, Adam. 2015. A Grammar of Xong. PhD dissertation, University at Buffalo (SUNY). 657 pp. (published 2021 as Mouton Grammar Library 84, De Gruyter, doi:10.1515/9783110764932)
sources.access_detail: copy on file; access check: open copy online (also: harvard online access (harvardkey))
sources.note: Describes WESTERN Xiangxi Miao (Fenghuang County, Yankan/La'ershan; ISO mmr), not muq. Ch. 3 Phonology never uses the word 'stress': 'the syllable is the most important unit of analysis in Xong phonology. The syllable is the only tone-bearing unit in Xong' (3.1, p. 57); 'tone is primarily a syllable-level phenomenon' with eight lexical tones (3.5, p. 94); sec. 3.6 'A note on non-tonal suprasegmental phenomena' (pp. 116-117) posits only a phrase-level intonational system (toneless particles/interjections, utterance-final fall, emphasis/focus by 'exaggerating' tones). Sec. 2.2.2 (pp. 16-18) sum…

sources.citation: Ratliff, Martha. 2010. Hmong-Mien Language History. Canberra: Pacific Linguistics 613 (open access, CC-BY, hdl:1885/146760)
sources.note: Family-level historical work; nothing on Xiangxi Miao stress. Only stress mentions: quotes Downer (1961:539) that Mien reduced syllables 'have weaker stress and shorter duration than the following full syllables so that a strong iambic rhythm is imparted to disyllabic words' (p. 28), and states Hmong-Mien nominal prefixes 'are unstressed' (sec. 4.2.1). Jiwei (Western Xiangxi) appears only as a comparative data point.
